strengths: The per-orientation heatmaps reveal structured generalization patterns that average accuracy obscures. These findings offer identifiable value to researchers studying viewpoint robustness and learned representations.

The fully-seen/partially-seen paradigm provides a useful controlled experiment. Keeping the baseline training budget at 200,000 images and repeating experiments with five random instance partitions strengthens the evidence for effects of training diversity.

Experiments cover three object categories, three architectures, cross-category transfer, pretraining, and rotation augmentation. This breadth supports the conclusion that the observed behavioral patterns recur across several tested conditions.

The small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette components provide an interpretable descriptive account of the accuracy patterns. Component ablations are informative, and the illustrated experimental setup communicates the central observations clearly.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central mechanistic claims exceed the evidence. Figures 4 and S.7 show associations among activation summaries, accuracy, and fully-seen/partially-seen responses; they do not establish that shared-feature neurons cause invariance to transfer between instances. Common dependence on visual similarity could also explain these associations. Targeted interventions with matched controls would strengthen the causal interpretation; alternatively, the abstract and discussion should present dissemination as a hypothesis consistent with the observations and keep the biological comparison explicitly analogical. This gap drives the leaning-reject recommendation despite the useful behavioral results.

Necessary: The invariance measurement needs validation or a narrower interpretation. Equations 5–8 compare activations averaged over entire orientation sets. Equal means can arise from strongly orientation-selective responses, so a high score does not establish stable neuronal responses across viewpoints. Moreover, requiring both set means to exceed the 95th-percentile threshold excludes units that respond strongly in-distribution but lose their response outside it. Report per-orientation variability or pairwise invariance, retained-unit counts, and threshold sensitivity, or restrict the conclusions to similarity of selected mean responses.

Necessary: Predictive validity is unresolved. Section 4.2 fits the logistic parameters by optimizing Pearson correlation, while Figures 3b and S.5 report that correlation without describing a held-out evaluation. The reported correlations above 0.8 therefore support a descriptive fit but do not establish performance on independent observations. Specify the fitting/evaluation separation and provide held-out validation, or consistently describe the model as descriptive. The generalizable/non-generalizable partition, derived from this fitted model using a 10% threshold, also needs a sensitivity analysis before supporting categorical conclusions.

Necessary reporting clarification: Specify test-image sampling, observations per orientation cubelet, and the meaning of error bars. Reconcile the statistical units in Figures 4b–c with Equations 7–8: the text describes points as instances or orientations, whereas the equations aggregate over neurons, instances, and orientation sets. This ambiguity makes the correlation evidence difficult to assess and reproduce.

Optional: Evaluate sensitivity to uniform sampling on SO(3), since uniform Euler-angle sampling does not yield uniform rotations. Varied rendering conditions would also help establish the breadth of the observations. Such extensions are optional if conclusions are scoped to novel views of training instances under the tested synthetic conditions.
